data.raw_text:
Road safety advocate James Deakin recently found himself in a public tussle with the Land Transportation Office (LTO) over what he called “inflated” traffic charges against his son.

On Dec. 18, 19-year-old Daniel missed the Quezon City exit on Skyway. He turned too late and crossed a double yellow line, leading to his apprehension and a citation for reckless driving.

Under Republic Act No. 4136, reckless driving is defined as operating a motor vehicle “without reasonable caution considering the width, traffic, grades, crossings, curvatures, visibility, weather, or other conditions of the highway, or so as to endanger the property or the safety or rights of any person or excessive or unreasonable damage to the highway."

By both definition and circumstance, the violation stands. Deakin cried foul, questioning the “very arbitrary decision” that could affect Daniel’s records and, potentially, his employment, insurance, and travel. “Will my son have a criminal record for changing lanes?” he told ABS-CBN News.

But as the old adages go: dura lex sed lex; the law may be harsh, but it is the law. And ignorance of the law excuses no one.

Daniel was given 15 days to pay a ₱2,000 fine and retrieve his license. But with weekends and holidays counted, that window effectively collapsed during the Christmas break. When the Deakins returned on Jan. 5, 2026, they encountered shifting requirements and bureaucratic delays—only to be told the deadline had lapsed and the penalty had escalated to a one-month suspension.

Worse, the vehicle Daniel was driving was later flagged as unregistered. In a separate post, Deakin bared it was a loaner accepted “in good faith,” citing the presence of a conduction sticker and temporary plate. However, Daniel failed to present an OR/CR at the time of apprehension, only a sales invoice from importer to dealer—and not from dealer to buyer.

Any way you slice it, an unregistered vehicle should not have been on the road at all.

That said, the LTO’s processes demand scrutiny. Deadlines that include holidays when offices are closed, requirements that surface mid-transaction, and penalties that escalate without a realistic chance to comply raise legitimate concerns.

Still, Deakin’s decision to take the issue public invites its own criticism. What could have been resolved through formal remedies was instead elevated to the so-called Supreme Court of Facebook.

Perhaps that’s the deeper issue. When processes are unclear and slow, people turn to social media spectacle instead of due process—even when they themselves apparently share fault.

There are no heroes and villains in this story. But the takeaway is simple: Accountability should apply to everyone: consistently and clearly, sans the need to go viral.

(✍️ Nikko Miguel Garcia)

#radarPH
